summary.text: Take the explicit case $p=7$ and $r=6$. A modular summation modulo $7^{25}$, tracking the $7$-adic valuation and unit part of each binomial factor, gives $a(7^6)\equiv821327337676838434975$ and $a(7^5)\equiv1012908569057404849376$, whose difference is $-7^{24}$ and hence is not divisible by $7^{25}$.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
a(n)=\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}\binom nk^2\binom{n+k-1}{k}^2.
\]
We give a counterexample with
\[
p=7,\qquad r=6.
\]
Here
\[
7^6=117649,\qquad 7^5=16807,
\]
and the modulus asserted by the conjecture is
\[
7^{4r+1}=7^{25}=1341068619663964900807.
\]
We will calculate both relevant sums modulo this number. The result is
\[
\begin{aligned}
a(117649)&\equiv 821327337676838434975\pmod{7^{25}},\\
a(16807)&\equiv 1012908569057404849376\pmod{7^{25}}.
\end{aligned}
\]
The difference of these two least nonnegative residues is exactly
\[
1012908569057404849376-821327337676838434975
 =191581231380566414401=7^{24}.
\]
Since \(7^{25}\nmid 7^{24}\), the two values are not congruent modulo \(7^{25}\). It remains to explain fully how the two displayed modular evaluations are obtained and why the finite recurrence used for them computes the defining sum.

Put
\[
M=7^{25}=1341068619663964900807.
\]
For every positive integer \(x\), write
\[
x=7^{\nu(x)}x^*,
\]
where \(\nu(x)=\nu_7(x)\) and \(7\nmid x^*\). Thus \(x^*\) is the \(7\)-free part of \(x\). All the factors to which this notation is applied below are positive.

For fixed \(n\), define
\[
C_k=\binom nk,\qquad D_k=\binom{n+k-1}{k}
\]
for \(0\leq k\leq n\). We keep a six-component state
\[
(k,e,u,f,v,s).
\]
Its intended meaning is
\[
\begin{aligned}
e&=\nu(C_k),& u&\equiv C_k^*\pmod M,\\
f&=\nu(D_k),& v&\equiv D_k^*\pmod M,\\
s&\equiv \sum_{i=0}^{k-1}C_i^2D_i^2\pmod M.
\end{aligned}
\]
All modular representatives used in the computation are chosen in the interval \([0,M-1]\).

At \(k=0\), both binomial coefficients are \(1\), and the partial sum is empty. Therefore the initial state is
\[
(0,0,1,0,1,0).
\]

Suppose that the state at index \(k<n\) has the asserted meaning. First append the \(k\)-th summand. Since
\[
C_k=7^e C_k^*,\qquad D_k=7^f D_k^*,
\]
we have
\[
C_k^2D_k^2=7^{2e+2f}(C_k^*)^2(D_k^*)^2.
\]
Consequently we update the partial sum by
\[
s'\equiv s+7^{2e+2f}u^2v^2\pmod M.
\]
There are two cases in carrying this out:

* If \(2e+2f<25\), the displayed term is evaluated and reduced modulo \(M\).
* If \(2e+2f\geq25\), it is divisible by \(7^{25}=M\), so its residue is zero and one simply sets \(s'=s\).

This case split avoids manipulating unnecessarily large powers and is mathematically exact.

The binomial identities needed to move from index \(k\) to index \(k+1\) are
\[
C_{k+1}(k+1)=C_k(n-k)
\]
and
\[
D_{k+1}(k+1)=D_k(n+k).
\]
The second follows directly from
\[
\binom{n+k}{k+1}=\binom{n+k-1}{k}\frac{n+k}{k+1}.
\]
Taking \(7\)-adic valuations in these identities gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
e'&=e+\nu(n-k)-\nu(k+1),\\
f'&=f+\nu(n+k)-\nu(k+1).
\end{aligned}
\]
Although these formulas are written using subtraction, the results are nonnegative because they are precisely the valuations of the positive integers \(C_{k+1}\) and \(D_{k+1}\).

After removing the powers of \(7\) from the same identities, we obtain
\[
\begin{aligned}
C_{k+1}^*(k+1)^*&=C_k^*(n-k)^*,\\
D_{k+1}^*(k+1)^*&=D_k^*(n+k)^*.
\end{aligned}
\]
The number \((k+1)^*\) is not divisible by \(7\), so it has a multiplicative inverse modulo \(M\). Hence the unit-part updates are
\[
\begin{aligned}
u'&\equiv u\,(n-k)^*\bigl((k+1)^*\bigr)^{-1}\pmod M,\\
v'&\equiv v\,(n+k)^*\bigl((k+1)^*\bigr)^{-1}\pmod M.
\end{aligned}
\]
The complete next state is therefore
\[
(k+1,e',u',f',v',s').
\]

This proves by induction on \(k\) that every state produced by the recurrence has the intended meaning. In particular, after the update at \(k=n-1\), the final partial-sum component is
\[
s_n\equiv\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}\binom nk^2\binom{n+k-1}{k}^2=a(n)\pmod M.
\]
Thus only finite integer arithmetic remains.

For completeness, the auxiliary operations in that arithmetic can be implemented without any division in the residue ring. To find \(\nu(x)\) and \(x^*\), repeatedly divide \(x\) by \(7\) while it is divisible by \(7\). In the present two calculations every number that is stripped is one of \(n-k\), \(k+1\), or \(n+k\), with \(n\leq7^6\) and \(0\leq k<n\). Hence it is positive and less than \(7^7\), so at most six divisions by \(7\) are needed.

To compute the inverse of a number \(q\) not divisible by \(7\), begin with its inverse modulo \(7\), using
\[
1^{-1}=1,\quad2^{-1}=4,\quad3^{-1}=5,\quad
4^{-1}=2,\quad5^{-1}=3,\quad6^{-1}=6
\pmod7.
\]
Starting from this value \(x_0\), perform five Newton updates
\[
x_{j+1}\equiv x_j(2-qx_j)\pmod M.
\]
Indeed,
\[
q\,x_j(2-qx_j)-1=-(qx_j-1)^2.
\]
Thus, if \(qx_j-1\) is divisible by \(7^t\), the next error is divisible by \(7^{2t}\). Beginning with divisibility by \(7\), after five updates the error is divisible by \(7^{32}\), and therefore in particular by \(7^{25}\). The resulting number is exactly \(q^{-1}\pmod M\). This supplies every inverse occurring in the recurrence using only multiplication, subtraction, and reduction modulo \(M\).

We now record the finite computation. Each row below gives an index \(k\) and the partial-sum residue
\[
s_k\equiv\sum_{i=0}^{k-1}C_i^2D_i^2\pmod M
\]
obtained by the recurrence.

For \(n=117649=7^6\), the checkpoints are
\[
\begin{array}{r|r}
k&s_k\\ \hline
10000&751418738924149166319\\
20000&480389004682122920602\\
30000&735485293131255042069\\
40000&522620957191632684477\\
50000&1335463077230015525471\\
60000&1134714729892139929772\\
70000&261517306227816860313\\
80000&553589051905689559747\\
90000&541672495595882686463\\
100000&551331438780516217258\\
110000&35294217536867405628\\
117600&854965444135944010367\\
117649&821327337676838434975
\end{array}
\]
As a more detailed check on the last block, the full state at \(k=117600\) is
\[
\begin{aligned}
(&117600,
4,
435482929867602661647,
4,
822020794103336524017,\\
&\hspace{35mm}854965444135944010367).
\end{aligned}
\]
Applying the recurrence for the remaining \(49\) indices gives the final state
\[
\begin{aligned}
(&117649,
0,
1,
0,
1053715666652496881601,\\
&\hspace{35mm}821327337676838434975).
\end{aligned}
\]
The last component and the proved state invariant yield
\[
a(117649)\equiv821327337676838434975\pmod M.
\]

For \(n=16807=7^5\), the corresponding checkpoints are
\[
\begin{array}{r|r}
k&s_k\\ \hline
4000&88430044787317957746\\
8000&553092598880959669554\\
12000&1268919108916714141048\\
16000&1155238323566449612302\\
16800&1046546675516510424768\\
16807&1012908569057404849376
\end{array}
\]
Here the full state at \(k=16800\) is
\[
\begin{aligned}
(&16800,
4,
420965928057859930600,
4,
862657665945755541644,\\
&\hspace{35mm}1046546675516510424768).
\end{aligned}
\]
The seven remaining recurrence steps give
\[
\begin{aligned}
(&16807,
0,
1,
0,
833959623200883878602,\\
&\hspace{35mm}1012908569057404849376).
\end{aligned}
\]
Thus
\[
a(16807)\equiv1012908569057404849376\pmod M.
\]
All entries in these tables result from the explicitly stated operations: stripping powers of \(7\), applying the two valuation updates, multiplying the unit parts by the indicated modular inverses, adding the next summand in the case \(2e+2f<25\), omitting it in the case \(2e+2f\geq25\), and reducing modulo \(M\) after each operation.

Finally, both displayed terminal residues lie between \(0\) and \(M-1\), and
\[
\begin{aligned}
1012908569057404849376
 -821327337676838434975
 &=191581231380566414401\\
 &=7^{24}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Therefore their difference is not divisible by
\[
M=7^{25}=7\cdot7^{24}.
\]
It follows that
\[
a(7^6)\not\equiv a(7^5)\pmod{7^{25}}.
\]
Since \(7\) is prime, \(7\geq7\), \(6\geq2\), and \(4\cdot6+1=25\), this is an admissible instance of the universally quantified conjecture. Hence the conjecture is false.
